questions.question: What is requirements engineering?
questions.reference_answer: The process of establishing the services that the customer requires from a system and the constraints under which it operates and is developed.
key_points: establishing the services the customer requires
and the constraints under which the system operates and is developed

questions.question: What is the difference between user requirements and system requirements?
questions.reference_answer: User requirements are natural-language statements plus diagrams of the services and constraints, written for customers. System requirements are a structured document with detailed descriptions of functions, services and constraints, defining what should be implemented; they may be part of the contract.
key_points: user requirements: natural language plus diagrams, written for customers
system requirements may be part of a contract

questions.question: What are the three classifications of non-functional requirements?
questions.reference_answer: Product requirements (how the delivered product must behave, e.g. speed, reliability), organisational requirements (from organisational policies and procedures) and external requirements (from factors external to the system, e.g. interoperability, legislation).

questions.question: What are the generic activities of the requirements engineering process?
questions.reference_answer: Requirements elicitation, analysis, validation and management; in practice they are interleaved in an iterative process.

questions.question: What should a scenario include?
questions.reference_answer: A description of the starting situation, the normal flow of events, what can go wrong, other concurrent activities, and the state when the scenario finishes.

questions.question: What are the guidelines for writing requirements?
questions.reference_answer: Invent a standard format and use it for all requirements, use language consistently ('shall' for mandatory, 'should' for desirable), highlight key parts of the requirement, and avoid computer jargon.

questions.question: Why might a requirement be written vaguely at first and then in great detail later?
questions.reference_answer: Requirements serve a dual function: for a bid they must be abstract and open to interpretation so several contractors can propose solutions; once the contract is awarded, the contractor writes a detailed system definition that the client can validate.
key_points: abstract so several contractors can bid
detailed once the contract is awarded

questions.question: Why can a vague word in a requirement cause the developers to build the wrong thing?
questions.reference_answer: Ambiguous requirements may be interpreted differently by developers and users: e.g. 'search' meant searching all clinics for the user but searching a single chosen clinic for the developer.
key_points: example: 'search' across all clinics vs in one clinic

questions.question: Why can failing a non-functional requirement make a whole system useless?
questions.reference_answer: Non-functional requirements define system-wide properties and constraints such as reliability and response time; they may be more critical than functional requirements and can affect the overall architecture, so if they are not met the system may be useless.
key_points: define properties like reliability and response time
may be more critical than functional requirements
apply to the system as a whole / affect the architecture

questions.question: How do I turn 'the system should be easy to use' into something that can be tested?
questions.reference_answer: Replace the goal with a verifiable requirement using a measure, e.g. medical staff can use all functions after four hours of training and make on average no more than two errors per hour afterwards.
key_points: ease of use is a goal, not verifiable
a verifiable requirement uses an objective measure
example: four hours of training, at most two errors per hour

questions.question: Why do agile teams often skip writing a full requirements document?
questions.reference_answer: They argue it is a waste of time because requirements change quickly and the document is always out of date; they use incremental RE and user stories. This is problematic for critical systems or systems built by several teams.
key_points: requirements change quickly so the document is out of date
problematic for critical or multi-team systems

questions.question: Which measures can be used to specify reliability and robustness?
questions.reference_answer: Reliability: mean time to failure, probability of unavailability, rate of failure occurrence, availability. Robustness: time to restart after failure, percentage of events causing failure, probability of data corruption on failure.
key_points: probability of unavailability / rate of failure occurrence / availability
probability of data corruption on failure

questions.question: In the insulin pump table, what dose is computed when the sugar level is increasing and the rate of increase is stable or increasing?
questions.reference_answer: CompDose = round((r2 - r1)/4); if the rounded result is 0, CompDose = MinimumDose.
key_points: if the result is 0, use MinimumDose

questions.question: In the structured specification of the insulin pump, what are the inputs and where do they come from?
questions.reference_answer: Inputs are the current sugar reading (r2) and the previous two readings (r0 and r1); the current reading comes from the sensor and the others from memory.
key_points: previous two readings r0 and r1
r2 from the sensor, others from memory

questions.question: In the MHC-PMS use case diagram, which use cases is the Doctor connected to?
questions.reference_answer: View record, Edit record, Generate report and Setup consultation.

questions.question: and what are the problems with that kind of requirement?

history.content: Domain requirements come from the system's operational domain, for example a train control system has to take braking characteristics in different weather into account.

questions.reference_answer: Understandability: they are written in the domain's language, which software engineers often do not understand. Implicitness: domain specialists know the area so well that they do not make the requirements explicit.
key_points: understandability: domain language not understood by engineers
implicitness: specialists do not state them explicitly

history.content: What is a system requirements specification?
It describes the functional and non-functional requirements of the system in more detail than the user requirements.

questions.reference_answer: Natural language, structured natural language, design description languages, graphical notations (e.g. UML use case and sequence diagrams) and mathematical specifications.

questions.question: What are the problems with writing requirements in natural language, and what is a structured specification?
questions.reference_answer: Problems: lack of clarity, requirements confusion (functional and non-functional mixed up) and amalgamation (several requirements expressed together). A structured specification limits the writer's freedom so requirements are written in a standard way; it suits embedded control systems but can be too rigid for business systems.
key_points: structured specification: standard way, limited freedom
good for embedded control, too rigid for business systems
